opus-5.5.text:
I think originality is a word that needs some care. In AI research today, almost nobody builds everything from zero. We all stand on a shared foundation: the Transformer, mixture-of-experts, the scaling-law mindset, and many open-source contributions. So for me, originality isn't about whether every component is new. It's about whether you found the problems that really matter at your scale and solved them in your own way.

For K2, a few things felt genuinely ours. One is the optimizer. We bet on Muon instead of the default AdamW, because we believed its token efficiency could be much better. But when you scale Muon to a trillion-parameter MoE model, you hit training instability, especially attention logits blowing up. So we developed what we call MuonClip, a QK-clip mechanism that keeps those logits under control. In the end we pretrained on more than fifteen trillion tokens without a single loss spike. That wasn't something we could copy from a paper; we had to get there through a lot of failed runs and careful thinking.

The second is how we think about the model's purpose. We designed K2 for agentic ability from the start, not just chatting. That meant building large-scale synthetic pipelines for tool-use data, simulating many environments and tools, and combining verifiable rewards with self-critique in reinforcement learning. The architecture choices served that too. For example, we used more experts and fewer attention heads, because we cared about long-context and inference efficiency in agent settings.

So I would describe our originality as taste plus execution. Taste means choosing which bets are worth making, like token efficiency, because high-quality data is becoming the bottleneck, so every token has to teach the model more. Execution means pushing those bets to work at the frontier.

And honestly, open-sourcing K2 is part of this too. If you believe your work has real technical substance, you should be comfortable letting the whole community examine it, build on it, and even challenge it. That's how the field moves forward.

r001.rationale: The candidate says K2 used Muon instead of AdamW and describes MuonClip, but it does not claim K2 was the first model at its scale trained with a matrix-orthogonalization-based non-Adam optimizer.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "originality" is a word people use a lot, but it's worth being precise about what it actually means in this field. If you look at the history of deep learning, almost nothing is original in the sense of appearing from nowhere. Transformers built on attention, attention built on sequence models, MoE goes back decades. So I don't think the right question is "did you invent something nobody had ever thought of." The right question is whether you made a real contribution to the frontier, something that moves the whole field forward and that other people then build on.

By that standard, I'm fairly comfortable with where K2 stands. Take Muon. The core optimizer idea came from the research community, and we were open about that. But nobody had taken it to a trillion-parameter scale, and when we tried, it didn't just work. We hit training instabilities, logits exploding, things that simply don't show up at small scale. The fix we developed, MuonClip with QK-clip, was not in any paper. That came out of our own engineering and our own experiments, and now you see other teams referencing it. That's what originality looks like in practice: you identify a promising direction, you push it past the point where others stopped, and you solve the problems that only appear when you push that far.

The same applies to the agentic data side. The idea of tool use isn't new, but building a large-scale synthetic pipeline where the model learns to actually complete multi-step tasks, with real environments and verifiable results, that was something we had to design ourselves. There wasn't a recipe to follow.

I'd also say we made a deliberate choice about where to be different and where not to be. There's a temptation to be different just to look different, to change architecture for its own sake. We didn't do that. Where DeepSeek's architecture was a good foundation, we used it, and we said so. Our bet was on the things we believed mattered most for the next stage: token efficiency, so you get more out of every piece of data, and agentic capability. Being concentrated on those bets, and getting them right, matters more to me than claiming novelty across the board.

And honestly, part of why we open-sourced K2 is that originality should be judged by the community, not by us. If people find value in the techniques, adopt them, and improve on them, that's the real test. So far that seems to be happening, and that's what I care about.

r001.rationale: The response says Muon had not previously been taken to trillion-parameter scale, implying a novel large-scale use, but it does not clearly state that Kimi K2 was the first model at its scale trained with a matrix-orthogonalization-based non-Adam optimizer.

astra-6.text:
I think originality has to be evaluated at several levels. There’s originality in a particular method, and there’s originality in how you bring methods together to build a capable system. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

For Kimi K2, I wouldn’t equate originality with having invented every component. The more useful questions are: What problems did we identify? Where did existing approaches fall short? And did our technical choices produce improvements that we can demonstrate?

At the same time, strong results alone don’t establish that something is original. You have to distinguish what builds on prior work from what is a new contribution. I think that’s the standard we should be held to: explain the choices clearly, acknowledge the foundations, and let the evidence support the claims.

r001.rationale: The response discusses originality and acknowledging prior work, but it does not state that Kimi K2 was tentatively the first publicly documented model at its scale trained with a matrix-orthogonalization-based non-Adam optimizer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think originality has to be discussed at the level of specific contributions. Building on existing research and doing original work aren’t mutually exclusive. The question is: what did we change, why did we change it, and can we demonstrate that it works?

For Kimi K2, I’d distinguish between originality in individual techniques and originality in bringing the whole system together. A model’s capabilities depend on many decisions working together, and that integration can involve substantial research. But it shouldn’t become a blanket claim that everything is new. The right approach is to give prior work credit and make our own contributions clear enough for others to examine.
